binders: q(x,t) is the state, with each component representing a conserved-quantity density; f is its physical flux function. [Printed p. 4, Section 1.1.1, (1.10) and following paragraph.]
x₁ and x₂ are any two spatial points serving as interval endpoints; t is time. The passage gives no explicit time domain or endpoint-order restriction. [Printed p. 4, sentence introducing (1.10).]

Grid cells carry cell integrals or cell averages; i−1 and i index two neighboring cells with averages Q_{i−1} and Q_i. No global index set is specified. [Printed p. 5, Section 1.2 and paragraph following (1.11).]
q_l and q_r are the constant left and right initial states in a Riemann problem, with its initial discontinuity placed at x = 0. [Printed p. 5, Section 1.2.1, (1.11).]
hypotheses: The integral balance concerns a conservation law whose interval total changes only through physical endpoint fluxes; nonconservative effects require additional source terms. [Printed p. 4, (1.10) and its explanation.]

Deriving the differential equation from (1.10) requires sufficient smoothness of q and f(q). This smoothness qualification is not imposed on the passage's discussion of discontinuous solutions satisfying integral conservation. [Printed pp. 4–5, Section 1.1.2.]
For the local finite volume workflow, Q_{i−1} and Q_i are cell averages in neighboring cells and the Riemann data are set to q_l = Q_{i−1} and q_r = Q_i. [Printed p. 5, paragraph following (1.11).]
The Riemann problem includes the hyperbolic equation together with the initial data, rather than initial data alone. [Printed p. 5, Section 1.2.1, opening definition.]
conclusions: For the stated conservation law, d/dt ∫_[x₁,x₂] q(x,t) dx = f(q(x₁,t)) − f(q(x₂,t)): the left endpoint flux enters with a plus sign and the right endpoint flux with a minus sign. [Printed p. 4, (1.10).]

At a discontinuity in q the differential equation does not hold in the classical sense, but the integral conservation law continues to hold. Discontinuities can develop even from smooth initial data. [Printed pp. 4–5, Section 1.1.2.]

Finite volume methods use integral conservation, approximate cell integrals or normalized cell averages, and modify these values at each time step through cell-edge fluxes. Their numerical flux functions approximate physical fluxes using the approximate cell averages available. [Printed p. 5, Section 1.2, first paragraph.]

Solving the Riemann problem with the neighboring cell averages as left and right states provides information that can be used to compute a numerical flux and update cell averages over a time step. [Printed p. 5, paragraph following (1.11).]

For hyperbolic problems the Riemann solution is described as typically depending on x/t alone and consisting of a finite set of waves propagating away from the origin with constant wave speeds. [Printed p. 5, Section 1.2.1, paragraph following (1.11).]

For linear hyperbolic systems, the Riemann problem is solved using eigenvalues and eigenvectors of A. The discussion extends the simple structure and construction of exact solutions or arbitrarily good approximations to nonlinear systems such as the Euler equations, and notes that approximate Riemann solvers are used in numerical implementations because exact nonlinear solutions are often expensive. [Printed pp. 5–6, Section 1.2.1.]
definitions_and_conventions: A cell average is the integral of q over the cell divided by the cell volume; it is distinguished from both an unnormalized integral and a pointwise grid value. [Printed p. 5, Section 1.2, first paragraph.]
Riemann initial data are q_l on x < 0 and q_r on x > 0 at t = 0. Equation (1.11) leaves the value at x = 0 unspecified. [Printed p. 5, (1.11).]
The choice x = 0 for the initial jump is introduced by 'say', indicating a chosen location for describing the Riemann problem. [Printed p. 5, sentence introducing (1.11).]

The physical flux f in the conservation equation and numerical flux functions in the finite volume method have distinct roles: the latter approximate the former from available approximate cell averages. [Printed p. 4, (1.10); printed p. 5, Section 1.2.]

contract_plain_english: The source states that conserved interval totals change through the physical left-minus-right endpoint flux, and that integral conservation remains fundamental for discontinuous solutions where the differential equation fails classically [printed pp. 4–5, (1.10), Section 1.1.2]. Finite volume methods approximate cell integrals or their volume-normalized averages and update these using numerical edge fluxes based on available approximate averages [printed p. 5, Section 1.2]. At a neighboring-cell interface, the averages supply the left and right piecewise constant Riemann data; solving that hyperbolic initial-value problem yields information usable for a numerical flux and a time-step update [printed p. 5, (1.11) and following paragraph]. This is a qualitative workflow without a specified flux formula, solver contract, or quantitative guarantee; approximate Riemann solvers are expressly allowed by the surrounding implementation discussion [printed pp. 5–6, Section 1.2.1].
